10214-introduction-to-the-philosophy-and:
Thomas Taylor wrote this guide to Plato as a defense of the Greek thinker as the chief guide to true philosophy. Taylor presents Plato not as one voice among many, but as the source from which later wisdom flows. His prose is grand and earnest, full of images of light, temples, and ascent toward the divine.

The book sketches Plato's life and thought, then maps his dialogues and key ideas for new readers. Virtue cleanses the passions, truth restores the soul, and study lifts the mind toward its proper good. Readers get a passionate, old-style doorway into Plato, useful even where they may not share Taylor's high claims.
10637-the-uprising-of-a-great-people-the:
Count Agenor de Gasparin, a French writer, published The Uprising of a Great People to explain the American Civil War to Europeans, and Mary L. Booth's translation appeared in a revised American edition in 1862. Gasparin argues that the North's uprising in 1861 was a moral stand for freedom, not a mere quarrel over tariffs or states' rights. A closing essay adds a word of peace on England and America.

The author revised his text to meet American reviewers and to speak to emancipation as the war's meaning sharpened. His book was read as prophecy by admirers on both sides of the ocean. Readers get a European liberal's view of the Union cause, written while the war's outcome was still unknown.
11308-the-book-of-enterprise-and-adventu:
This 1851 book for young people, in a new condensed edition illustrated by Absalon, aims to excite children to read by showing how perils can be surmounted with energy, patience, and self-reliance. Contents range from Arabian hospitality and crocodile shooting to the sagacity of the elephant, anecdotes of the tiger. the death of Sir John Moore, sketches in Virginia, an escape from a burning ship, and a visit to a penguin rookery. War and bloodshed are deliberately avoided.

The editor's preface states the moral plainly: stories should inspire heroic enthusiasm and dependence on Providence alongside self-sacrifice. The selection reflects a migrating, seafaring age, when readers might face flood and field themselves. As children's literature, it is adventure with a conscience, brisk and instructive.
11353-history-of-liberia-johns-hopkins-u:
J. H. T. McPherson's History of Liberia, ninth series number ten of the Johns Hopkins Studies in Historical and Political Science, abridges his doctoral dissertation into a brief 1891 sketch. Chapters trace the colonization idea and movement, Maryland in Liberia, the Republic of Liberia, and the historic significance of colonization as a Southern move toward emancipation. a check on the slave trade, a step toward African civilization, a missionary effort, and a refuge.

McPherson calls Liberia's west African corner the scene of experiments unique in history, from which knowledge must come for solving problems of African development. His tone is academic and of its time, sympathetic to colonization. Historians now read the study both for its facts and for its assumptions about race and empire.
11894-the-mahabharata-of-krishna-dwaipay:
Kisari Mohan Ganguli's English prose translation presents Book 3 of the Mahabharata, the Vana Parva, or Book of the Forest, from the original Sanskrit. The section opens with Janamejaya asking to hear the word Jaya, after bowing to Narayana, Nara, and the goddess Saraswati.

In the forest exile, the Pandava brothers and their mother Kunti endure grief and hardship, while figures such as Nakula and Sahadeva wait in silence to please their elders. Later passages follow disguised heroes, charioteers, and kings, including the story of Nala, as the epic turns forest wandering into a long education in duty, patience, and kingship.
11947-on-the-edge-of-the-war-zone-from-t:
Mildred Aldrich's On the Edge of the War Zone gathers letters written from her hilltop in France, from the Battle of the Marne to the entrance of the Stars and Stripes. Friends, old and new, had persistently asked for news of life on the hilltop after the battle, and their demands inspired the collecting and editing of these letters.

Aldrich writes of the walled cemetery at Chambry, scene of desperate fighting on September 6 and 7. Of gas warfare, noting that American men were protected against gas and that the enemy would use such weapons less freely after tasting their own medicine. The letters offer a civilian's close view of war, measured in villages, walls, and daily endurance.
12058-the-mahabharata-of-krishna-dwaipay:
Kisari Mohan Ganguli translated this fourth book of the Mahabharata into English prose from Sanskrit in the late nineteenth century. Known as the Virata Parva, it covers the thirteenth year of the Pandava brothers exile, when they must live undiscovered or face another long banishment.

Yudhishthira and his brothers take humble posts at the court of King Virata, while Draupadi serves the queen in disguise. The tale builds through near discoveries, court intrigue, and insults that test their patience. It ends in open battle, when the Kaurava army raids Virata cattle and Arjuna, still hidden, must fight alone. The book thus turns a year of waiting into a test of disguise, honor, and restraint.
12106-old-gorgon-graham-more-letters-fro:
George Horace Lorimer's Old Gorgon Graham, more letters from a self-made merchant to his son, published in 1903 with pictures by F. R. Gruger and Martin Justice, continues the elder Graham's advice. An illustration shows exchanging the grip of the third degree. The contents open with a letter from John Graham, head of the house of Graham and Company, pork packers in Chicago.

The letters that follow, from a son to his father and back, mix business counsel with moral warning: work hard, distrust flattery, save money, and judge men by conduct. Lorimer, editor of the Saturday Evening Post, made Graham a popular philosopher of American business, whose gruff humor carried serious advice about character.
12333-the-mahabharata-of-krishna-dwaipay:
Kisari Mohan Ganguli translated this third book of the Mahabharata, the Vana Parva, into English prose from Sanskrit in the late nineteenth century. This part two continues from a previous volume at section one hundred forty-five.

The forest book follows the Pandava brothers in exile, with Bhima strength scattering birds and beasts: ruddy geese, gallinules, ducks, parrots, herons, and elephants in confusion flee before him. A mid-book passage tells how the Krauncha hill, son of Himavat, was rent asunder, which is why swans and vultures now migrate to Sumeru mountains. The Vana Parva mixes battles, pilgrimages, and moral tales. Ganguli translation made the epic accessible to English readers.
12350-the-international-jewish-cook-book:
Florence Kreisler Greenbaum, instructor in cooking and domestic science, published The International Jewish Cook Book in a second edition in 1919. The book holds sixteen hundred recipes according to Jewish dietary laws, with rules for kashering.

Recipes come from America, Austria, Germany, Russia, France, Poland, Roumania, and beyond, covering soups, meats, fish, vegetables, and baked goods. A mid-book receipt for crescent rolls rolls risen dough into a square sheet, spreads melted butter, cuts six-inch squares, and bakes them light in a hot oven. Greenbaum writes for housekeepers keeping kosher in America. The book is a landmark of Jewish American cookery, practical and wide-ranging.
13349-christianity-its-evidences-its-ori:
Annie Besant's Freethinker's Text-Book, Part 2, sets out to reject Christianity after close examination. She promises to test its evidences, trace its origin and growth, judge its morality and dogmas, study its supposed founder, and follow its symbols and ceremonies. The foundation, she says, was already shaken in Part 1.

Besant weighs Gospel sayings against tradition, counts how seldom early writers name the times and places of the Gospel story. She compares Christian ideas with Mithras, the reconciler who brings the Word and redeems the world. Her case is argumentative and learned, aimed at readers ready to doubt. It stands as a full Victorian freethought attack on a faith she finds unproven.
13533-the-unfolding-life-a-study-of-deve:
Antoinette Abernethy Lamoreaux studies child development for religious training in The Unfolding Life, 1907, with an introduction by Marion Lawrance. She moves from fundamental principles through early childhood, the junior age of nine to twelve, and adolescence, showing how a child grows toward faith step by step.

Rows of chrysanthemums, roses, lilies, and orchids open the book as an image of unfolding variety. Young children imitate with exact care, then learn to emulate a hero's spirit, and later to stand with public opinion or bravely against it. A mission Sunday school talk on habits, using cement walks as an example, shows Lamoreaux's teaching method: truth seen and felt must impel action.
13615-studies-in-the-psychology-of-sex-v:
Havelock Ellis's sixth study, Sex in Relation to Society, turns from the sexual impulse and its object to third persons, community, and ancient traditions. Previous volumes, he says, left out environmental influences that powerfully affect impulse and its gratification, and this volume must face them.

Ellis discusses abstinence, nervous disturbance, and the reported benefits of regulated intercourse in neurasthenic women, always as opinions held by others rather than as his own prescription. Marriage customs follow, including couples married but not parsoned, and Venezuelan births outside official marriage blamed on wedding costs, not laxity. The book is a sober survey of sex, law, and custom.
13634-the-continental-monthly-vol-1-no-2:
The Continental Monthly for February 1862, devoted to literature and national policy, opens in the Civil War with Our War and Our Want. It asks whether the republic can exist with slavery in it, insists the war has gone too far to retreat. It seeks an honest course to conquer the foe, re-establish the Union, and secure future prosperity.

French Protestant refugees, wounded in battle yet cheering men onward to glory, later melt into English life until pure Saxon blood is hard to find. Runaway slaves in swamps, never betrayed by fellow workers, die in huts and are buried where they lay. The magazine joins war policy, Huguenot history, and slavery's human cost in one wartime number.
146-a-little-princess-being-the-whole-st:
Sara Crewe comes to Miss Minchin's London school with a loving father and a rich imagination. Frances Hodgson Burnett's Little Princess follows Sara from pampered pupil to attic servant when her father dies in India. Miss Minchin strips her of comfort and sets her to hard work.

Sara befriends Ermengarde, Lottie, and Becky, and shares scraps and stories with them. An Indian gentleman next door, aided by Ram Dass, secretly feeds and warms her attic. The magic of kindness restores her fortunes in the end. The novel teaches that a princess is made by manner, not money.
15581-life-of-tecumseh-and-of-his-brothe:
Benjamin Drake, author of The Life of Black Hawk, published this life of Tecumseh and his brother the Prophet in Cincinnati in 1841, with E. Morgan and Company. A historical sketch of the Shawanoe Indians heads the volume, naming Catahecassa or Black-Hoof, Cornstalk, and Spemica-Lawba, the High Horn, or Captain Logan.

Chapters trace Tecumseh's parentage, his sister Tecumapease, and brothers including Tenskwautawa the Prophet, then his birthplace, the destruction of the Piqua village, and his first battle. Later parts follow battles on the Little Miami and Paint Creek, Fort Recovery, and the Rapids of the Maumee. Drake also records the Prophet's mission, with four strings of beads said to be made of his flesh, shaken as a solemn pledge. The book is an early American Indian biography, detailed and of its time.
16014-the-hedge-school-the-midnight-mass:
Three Irish tales by William Carleton, part three of Traits and Stories of the Irish Peasantry, in volume three of his works. The Hedge School, The Midnight Mass, and The Donagh, or The Horse Stealers, share the volume. Carleton writes from inside the cabins he knew, with humour and anger in equal part. His tales defend the Irish peasantry against English scorn.

The Hedge School opens by denying a calumny: that Irish peasants cared nothing for education. Lower orders of no country, Carleton insists, showed such a positive inclination for learning, even under hardship. The Midnight Mass and The Donagh follow, with faith, theft, and village justice. The volume stands as a classic defence: a people, poor but book-hungry, told true.
16361-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
October 1877 brings Lippincott's Magazine of Popular Literature and Science, volume twenty, number one hundred eighteen, opening with Chester and the Dee in two papers. The history of Chester, the essay says, is that of a key. It was the last city to give up Harold's cause to William the Conqueror. It was also the last to fall for the Stuart king against the Parliamentarians. In Roman times the Twentieth Legion, Valens Victrix, held it as the key of dominion in Britain's northwest.

An illustration of the Dee above Bala and a smiling Percival accompany the travel writing. Lippincott's mixed such history, fiction, and science for a general American audience. This number offers a pleasant sample of Victorian magazine travel and antiquarian lore.
1657-crito:
Plato's Crito, translated by Benjamin Jowett, records Socrates in prison, visited by his friend Crito, who urges escape before the death sentence is carried out. Socrates refuses, in a short, powerful argument. Jowett, master of Balliol College, Oxford, translated Plato for English students.

He asks whether one should obey the laws even when they condemn unjustly, and whether escape would betray the city that raised him. The dialogue remains a founding text on law, duty, and conscience. Crito, a short dialogue, pairs with the Apology and Phaedo as Socrates' last days.
16858-wit-humor-reason-rhetoric-prose-po:
George W. Bain wrote this 1915 book of eight popular lectures, issued by the Pentecostal Publishing Company in Louisville and dedicated to his wife Anna M. Bain. His introduction claims no literary merit or new thought; the lectures aim to do good, as they did from the platform. Hearers said the talks shaped their lives, and Bain hoped readers would gain the same help when his voice fell silent.

Bain mixes wit, humor, reason, rhetoric, prose, poetry, and story, with a speaker's care for grip on his hearers over grammar. His lectures are earnest, moral, and full of anecdotes. The book gives a sample of popular pulpit oratory in 1915, useful for readers of preaching history and of old-style public speaking.
17162-mother-stories-from-the-old-testam:
This 1908 Altemus volume retells Old Testament tales for mothers to read to children, with forty-five pictures. Adam and Eve, Cain and Abel, the Flood, the Tower of Babel, and Lot's flight open the set. Abraham and Isaac, Joseph and his brothers, Moses, Joshua, Gideon, Samson, Ruth, and David and Goliath follow in short, plain chapters.

Each tale is kept brief and clear, with morals kept light and language fit for young ears. The book belongs to a series of mother stories on nature, fairy tales, and the New Testament. Families who want Bible stories in storybook form will find a handy, well pictured first set here.
17163-mother-stories-from-the-new-testam:
This 1906 Altemus volume retells New Testament tales for mothers to read to children, with forty-five pictures. The wise men's visit, the angel's tidings, and Jesus in the temple open the set. Parables follow: the sower, the leaven, hidden treasure, the pearl, the net, the good shepherd, the lost coin, and the prodigal son, with healings, feedings, and the walk on the sea between.

Each tale stays brief and plain, fit for young ears and bedtime reading. The book pairs with its Old Testament sister volume in the same series. Families who want New Testament stories in storybook form will find a handy, well pictured first set, gentle in tone and easy to follow.
17408-the-florentine-painters-of-the-ren:
Bernhard Berenson's Florentine Painters of the Renaissance, third edition revised and enlarged, studies painting from Giotto to Michelangelo. Orcagna, Masaccio, Fra Filippo, Pollaiuolo, Verrocchio, Leonardo, and Botticelli lead the essay, set beside Venetian rivals from the Bellini to Tintoretto. An index to the works of the principal Florentine painters, and an index of places, close the volume.

Berenson argues that Florentines were sculptors, architects, poets, and men of science besides painters, so painting alone gives only a partial view. His prose is learned yet lively, with connoisseur's judgments on every page. Art lovers will find a classic guide to Florence's golden age, still sharp for museum visits today.
18175-yorksher-puddin-a-collection-of-th:
John Hartley wrote Yorksher Puddin', a set of the most popular dialect stories from his pen, printed by W. Nicholson and Sons. Hartley, author of Yorkshire Ditties, dedicates the book to his sister Hannah, to whose motherly care he owes more than he can repay.

Stories run from Frozen to Death and the cottage on the hill to spirit rapping, a mule in the garden, tinkling Tom, and a new school board. A Christmas Eve circle begs Uncle John for a tale, and Hartley obliges in broad Yorkshire speech. The book is warm, funny, and homely, best read aloud, slowly, for the full flavor of the dialect.
18292-s-o-s-stand-to:
Sergeant Reginald Grant wrote this 1918 memoir of three years in the artillery of the First Canadian Division. Grant served in the First Field Artillery Brigade, and he dedicates the book to the lads of his Sacrifice Battery who died, and to his brothers Gordon and Billy, still fighting. His stated aim is to lay out the division's movement as seen through his own duties.

The chapters follow the war in order: the first night, Ypres, Sanctuary Woods, the Somme, and Vimy, with lighter chapters on a bath under difficulties, bees and honey, and a horse. Shells, gas, mud, and humor mix in the telling. Readers get a soldier's view of the Western Front, told by a gunner who stayed with his battery from first action to last.
18554-the-continental-monthly-vol-5-no-2:
This February 1864 issue of the Continental Monthly, a journal devoted to literature and national policy, appeared in the middle of the Civil War. Its lead article looks at Thomas Jefferson as seen by the light of 1863, tracing how Federalist writers abused him in life while Democratic papers praised him without measure. The writer notes how later readers canonized Jefferson as the apostle of American democracy.

The issue also weighs how the war had shattered old party cries about the Union as it was. Readers get a sharp period view of Jefferson's fame and of wartime politics. The monthly stands as a useful source for Civil War era thought.
18946-the-continental-monthly-vol-4-no-6:
The December 1863 number of The Continental Monthly presents a magazine devoted to literature and national policy in the middle of the American Civil War. Its opening essay speaks of Americans as empire builders, called to create on new soil rather than to destroy. That confident national voice runs through the number.

Inside, readers find essays, stories, and commentary written while the war's outcome was still uncertain. Literature and politics sit side by side, as the editors meant them to. The issue gives modern readers a direct sense of how educated Northern readers argued about the nation's purpose, its future, and the war being fought in their name.
20455-the-true-story-of-our-national-cal:
The True Story of Our National Calamity of Flood, Fire and Tornado was rushed out after a string of American disasters. Floods, fires, and tornadoes had struck town after town. The book promised the full account of the damage and the suffering.

Its pages include a prayer for those caught in the calamity. It asks God to let the stricken know the comfort of His presence, and to stir His people to give generous aid for their needs. Such instant histories mixed news, pictures, and devotion, and they were sold to help readers grasp losses too large for headlines.
20647-the-continental-monthly-vol-2-no-3:
The Continental Monthly for September 1862, volume 2, number 3, appeared while the Civil War ground through its second year. The magazine mixed literature with national policy. Among its essays stands an assessment of the English historian Henry Thomas Buckle, who had just died.

Buckle was born in London in the early part of 1824, the essay notes. He was consequently about thirty-eight years old at the time of his death. His father was a wealthy, thoroughly educated gentleman of the metropolis. The essay weighs Buckle's vast History of Civilization and the promise cut short by his early death.
20899-the-continental-monthly-vol-2-no-5:
Great convulsions must root in far past times, argues The Continental Monthly for November 1862. The Civil War then shaking the continent drew force from wide fields of feeling. Volume two, number five opens with that grave, searching claim.

The Continental Monthly served the Union cause with tales, poems, and essays. Each number mixed war thought with letters and art for home readers. Its pages show a North at war, thinking hard about why it fought. This issue freezes one month of that strain, when the war's end still lay far beyond sight or sure hope.
20904-the-right-stuff-some-episodes-in-t:
A young Scot sleeps away from his native hillside for the first time in The Right Stuff. Ian Maclaren, in tales of a North Briton's career, tracks that raw start. No town of three thousand folk, no train rides, had yet shaped the lad.

London pies, city ways, and hard knocks school him as the tale rolls on. Maclaren, famed for Beside the Bonnie Brier Bush, writes with Scots warmth. His hero's grit, the right stuff of the title, carries him upward. Readers meet a coming-of-age tale in the old mould: green youth, stern world, and character proved by use.
21984-kemps-nine-daies-wonder-performed-:
A clown dances from London to Norwich in Will Kemp's Nine Daies Wonder. The Camden Society reprinted his morris dance pamphlet in 1840. Alexander Dyce supplies the introduction and notes. Kemp was a comic actor of high reputation, successor to Tarlton in the Queen's favor and the audience's. He played the Clown in Shakespeare's company before this solo feat made him a legend.

In 1600 Kemp danced the whole road in nine days of actual dancing, and wrote his own account to answer doubters. The old spelling stands as printed, macrons and all. Dyce's notes untangle the people and places along the road. The little book is a jewel of Elizabethan popular culture: a stunt, a boast, and a dance, all documented.
22049-a-literary-history-of-the-english-:
J. J. Jusserand, a French scholar who knew England well, wrote A Literary History of the English People. He begins by comparing the two nations across the Channel. England's people, like France's, formed from several races layered one on another. The mix differed, and so, Jusserand argues, did the genius of each nation.

From those origins he follows English writing through its early centuries. Poetry, chronicle, and drama are tied to the life of the people who made them. Jusserand writes as a friendly foreigner, learned but clear. His history won respect in both countries and still shows how the Victorians understood the roots of English literature.
22074-the-doings-of-the-fifteenth-infant:
The Doings of the 15th Infantry Brigade records a British brigade's first months in the Great War. Its commander wrote the account from his own diary and orders. The brigade went to France in August 1914 with the original expeditionary force. It fought through the retreat from Mons and the advance that followed into 1915.

The commander explains that the diary was pruned of private matters before print. What remains is a working record of marches, billets, attacks, and losses. He resisted adding hindsight, so the fog of those months stays in the text. Brigade histories like this one preserve the war as its officers actually saw it, day by day.
22926-the-continental-monthly-vol-6-no-3:
New York's Continental Monthly speaks from September 1864 in this issue, volume 6, number 3. One essay takes up the evils of domestic service. These evils, the writer warns, are so varied and deep-rooted that even the stoutest reformer stands appalled. Groans over them are plenty, thoughtful study of their causes is rare.

The magazine mixed literature, politics, and reform during the Civil War's hardest years. Essays, poems, and sketches addressed a Union readership living through draft calls and casualty lists. A single issue shows the range, household complaints beside national crisis. For modern readers the value is texture. It preserves what educated Americans argued about while the war ground through its third autumn.
23689-the-continental-monthly-vol-6-no-5:
The Continental Monthly for November 1864, devoted to literature and national policy, appeared in the third year of the American Civil War. Its leading article, The Progress of Liberty in the United States, takes up the question of whether the war was necessary. It answers those in the loyal states who clamored for peace at any price.

The writer sorts the peace men into three classes. First come the ignorant, who do not know what the conflict is about. Then come the better informed, who see no moral clash between free society and slave society. Last come the demagogues, who would use both groups to force surrender. Drawing on the census of 1860, the article argues that the Slave Power brought the war on itself. It is a sharp piece of wartime political writing.
23776-the-school-of-recreation-1684-edit:
R. H. published The School of Recreation in London in 1684, a gentleman's tutor to the most ingenious exercises of the age. Printed for Henry Rodes near Bride Lane in Fleet Street, it promises to teach a gentleman how to spend his leisure well, in an age when recreation was itself an art.

Its exercises run from hunting, fishing, and hawking to racing, riding, and fowling. Shooting, bowling, tennis, cock-fighting, ringing, and billiards complete the list. The address to the reader frames man as an abridgement of creation, fallen from innocence yet still lord of his sports. For modern readers it is a vivid handbook of Restoration pastimes.
24491-the-continental-monthly-vol-6-no-6:
Published in December 1864, this sixth number of the sixth volume of The Continental Monthly was devoted to literature and national policy. The Civil War fills its pages, with a fifth paper on an army's organisation and movements. It argues that war is not all marches and battles, but long stretches of drill, camp life, and waiting.

Other pieces in the number treat the politics and letters of a nation at war. The magazine spoke to educated Northern readers who wanted argument, not only news. The issue gives a vivid sense of how Americans wrote and thought about the war in its last winter, before the fighting ended.
24890-the-prophete-ionas-with-an-introdu:
William Tyndale's Prophete Ionas gives the book of Jonah in early Tudor English, with a long introduction on how to read all of scripture. Tyndale, signing himself W. T., tells the Christian reader that hypocrites stop up the wells of scripture with traditions and false allegories, as the Philistines stopped Abraham's wells with earth.

His key image is plain: scripture has an outer bark for the fleshly mind to gnaw, and inner pith, sweetness, and life for God's elect. The Jonah text follows, with the prophet in the fish's belly praying his way back to hope. The book shows Tyndale the translator at work, putting the Bible into English for common readers.
25101-the-continental-monthly-vol-2-no-6:
The December 1862 number of the Continental Monthly, devoted to literature and national policy, speaks from the middle of the Civil War. Its leading discussion, the third part of a series on the Union, weighs President Lincoln's plan for gradual, compensated emancipation in loyal states against immediate emancipation everywhere.

Writers count the cost of buying freedom and compare the population, soil, climate, and shoreline of free and slave states. They argue that paid emancipation would cost less than a few months of war. The issue captures Northern debate at a turning point, months before the Emancipation Proclamation took full effect.
26077-the-continental-monthly-vol-3-no-2:
The February 1863 Continental Monthly, devoted to literature and national policy, opens on the Union's finances in extreme peril. Public debt already tops $720,000,000, with Treasury estimates near $1,122,000,000 by July 1863 and $1,744,000,000 a year later, while gold commands a premium of 32 percent over treasury notes.

Other pieces cover a trip to Antietam, American destiny, the birth of the lily, nullification and secession, and the Sioux War, with a serial tale continued. The issue's Union voice is plain: the Union and liberty will not be surrendered without a struggle, and its motto gleams on every blade, 'The Union shall be preserved.'
26216-the-son-of-monte-cristo:
The Son of Monte-Cristo, issued in New York in 1884, closes a continuation of Alexander Dumas's Count of Monte-Cristo, following an earlier volume called The Wife of Monte-Cristo. Its hero is Esperance, the Count's son, followed from boyhood onward, with his devotion to Jane Zeld at the heart of the romance. Scenes in Algeria carry a wild charm, from Esperance's abduction to his struggle with a sultan on a desert oasis.

Haydee's ordeal in the slave mart at Constantinople and the Count's own graphic episodes add colour. A Lorraine fair brings Iron Jaws, a giantess, a sword swallower, and a rope dancer. The book offers Dumas-style thrills in a new generation, with escapes, villains, and lovers reuniting against long odds.
26990-holy-in-christ-thoughts-on-the-cal:
Andrew Murray's Holy in Christ meditates on the calling of God's children to be holy as He is holy, taking its text from Scripture's command, I am holy: ye shall be holy. Murray, author of Abide in Christ, writes for believers who praise the holiness movement yet hold only vague thoughts of what holiness means.

The book teaches that holiness comes not from effort alone but from taking one's place in Christ and living in the power of the Spirit within. Its short chapters turn doctrine into daily practice, and it remains a standard devotional of the evangelical holiness tradition.
27262-mother-earth-vol-1-no-3-may-1906-m:
Mother Earth, volume one, number three, May 1906, is Emma Goldman's monthly magazine devoted to social science and literature, ten cents a copy and a dollar a year. Tidings of May mocks how human beings live nowadays, while the May sun gives life to beauty.

Whitman's Envy, Margaret Grant on This Man Gorky, and a piece on Comrade Maxim Gorky fill the early pages. Alexander Berkman, Voltarine de Cleyre's poem, and The White Terror follow. Schroeder on paternalistic government, Bolton Hall on liberty in common life, and Baginski on Hauptmann with the weavers of Silesia complete an anarchist miscellany.
28011-tomato-culture-a-practical-treatis:
Will W. Tracy of the Bureau of Plant Industry, United States Department of Agriculture, wrote Tomato Culture, published in New York by Orange Judd Company in 1907 and dedicated to Dr. F. M. Hexamer. The practical treatise covers the tomato's history, characteristics, planting, fertilization, cultivation in field, garden, and greenhouse, and harvesting.

Chapters treat soil, hotbeds, staking and pruning, varieties, seed breeding, canning, cost of production, insects, and diseases, with illustrations of flowers, fruits, and new varieties under test. Tracy's book is a standard early American guide to growing tomatoes for market and home.
29456-the-comic-latin-grammar-a-new-and-:
Written in 1840, this comic Latin grammar offers a new and facetious introduction to the tongue, meant to teach through laughter. Its text keeps old spelling and pronunciation notes, warning modern students that it predates new-style classical pronunciation. The letter j, for one, is not to be sounded as in jam today. Prosody marks long vowels with macrons and short vowels with breves.

The book jokes its way through declensions, conjugations, and verse, disarming criticism with a smile. A note warns that some of its material may offend modern readers. Students of Latin, humor, and Victorian schooling will find a lively, old-style primer that proves grammar need not be dull.
29777-the-identification-of-the-writer-o:
Printed in London in 1916, this short study takes up the strange unsigned letter sent to Lord Monteagle in 1605. The letter warned him away from the opening of Parliament on the fifth of November. It had no date, no name, and, as one old writer put it, almost no sense in it. Yet it helped unmask the Gunpowder Plot.

The author weighs the official story and tests the handwriting against a tract once held by Francis Tresham. He argues that the writer was William Vavasour, a dependant of the Tresham family. That claim is argued from the script and the ties between the families, not proved beyond doubt. Facsimiles let the reader judge the hand for himself.
29875-dreamers-of-the-ghetto:
I. Zangwill published Dreamers of the Ghetto with Harper and Brothers in 1898, in New York and London. Zangwill was already known for Children of the Ghetto, The Master, and The King of Schnorrers. The new book returns to the ghetto world of his earlier work, but its figures are dreamers rather than the children of his first ghetto book.

Zangwill writes with the splendid imagery and keen dissection of character his readers praised in The Master. The dreamers here live by visions, faiths, and ideals that set them apart from the crowd around them. The book is a set of portraits in story form, warm, sharp, and humane, about Jewish life and the minds that would remake it.
30040-the-red-river-colony-a-chronicle-o:
Louis Aubrey Wood wrote The Red River Colony, a chronicle of the beginnings of Manitoba, printed in Toronto in 1915. A frontispiece from a painting at St. Mary's Isle shows Thomas Douglas, fifth Earl of Selkirk. Wood dedicates the book to his father. Twelve chapters carry the colony's story from St. Mary's Isle and Selkirk the colonizer through the loosening of purse-strings, Stornoway and beyond, and wintering on the bay.

Red River and Pembina, the beginning of strife, and Colin Robertson the avenger follow. Seven Oaks, Lord Selkirk's journey, and Fort William lead to the pipe of peace. Plates show the Place d'Armes in Montreal in 1807 and Joseph Frobisher, a partner in the North-West Company. A bibliographical note and an index close a short, clear chronicle of settlement, rivalry, and the road to Manitoba.
30061-the-religious-sentiment-its-source:
Daniel G. Brinton wrote The Religious Sentiment: Its Source and Aim, a contribution to the science and philosophy of religion, printed in New York in 1876 by Henry Holt and Company. Brinton was a member of the American Philosophical Society and the American Philological Society. He had already written The Myths of the New World, a treatise on the symbolism and mythology of the red race of America. The transcriber kept a number of typographical errors, marked with notes.

Chapters run from the bearing of the laws of mind on religion through the emotional elements and the rational postulates of the religious sentiment. Prayer and its answer, the myth and the mythical cycles, and the cult with its symbols and rites follow. Brinton treats religion as a sentiment with a source and an aim, open to study by the laws of mind, emotion, reason, prayer, myth, and cult alike.
30085-life-of-henry-martyn-missionary-to:
Mrs. Sarah J. Rhea abridged the Life of Henry Martyn, Missionary to India and Persia, 1781 to 1812, from the memoir. It appeared in the Missionary Annals series, printed in Chicago in 1888 by the Woman's Presbyterian Board of Foreign Missions of the Northwest. Three sections order it: education and preparation, life in India, and life in Persia and death. Rhea opens with an album adorned with pictures of missionaries, her brethren and sisters, ambassadors of the King.

 Rhea's own missionary life, as companion of the man Dr. Perkins called the later Henry Martyn, was spent in Henry Martyn's Persia. The two Persian evangelists were alike in many things, and also in their deaths. Passing out of the Tabriz gate homeward after illness in the fated city, each rose to the heavenly city, leaving a foreign grave whose white stones, the Nestorians say, still speak out.
30168-a-history-of-giggleswick-school-fr:
Edward Allen Bell traces Giggleswick School from its foundation in 1499 to 1912, in a first edition published at Leeds in July 1912. Early chapters cover John Nowell, the Edward VI charter, and the free school. Its master and usher, the statutes of 1592, governors, scholars, and school hours are laid out in detail. Later chapters follow masters such as Christopher Shute and Robert Dockray, gifts and bequests, and the school's ties to Cambridge.

Bell, sometime scholar of Christ Church, Oxford, also surveys teaching in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, from Lily's Latin grammar and the trivium to Hebrew, music, and Puritan rule. The result is a dense local history, rich in names, rents, and rules, for readers who want one English school followed across four centuries without skipping its quarrels or its growth.
32820-world-beyond-pluto:
C. H. Thames sends Johnny Mayhem, the man of many bodies, on a pursuit beyond Pluto, in a story from Amazing Stories of November 1958. On Triton, stevedore foreman Pitchblend Hardesty loads an all-girl symphony orchestra at night, since the spaceport is busy with Neptune ore ships by day. A tolling bell announces a prison break from the Interstellar Penitentiary.

Mayhem follows the fugitive House Bartock, who has fled aboard the ship Mozart's Lady with Jane. The chase runs almost two billion miles from Neptune's orbit to Pluto's in three days. Mayhem travels in a tiny one-man coffin ship, barely room for a man lying flat, plus rations and water. On a snowy world beyond Pluto, blaster fire decides whether Bartock escapes or Mayhem brings him down.
33296-five-young-men-messages-of-yesterd:
Charles Reynolds Brown's Five Young Men, copyrighted in 1917, brings messages of yesterday to the young men of today. Brown, Dean of Yale's School of Religion, dedicates the book to the young men of Yale. Its contents open with the young man who was a favorite son, then take up other biblical youths as patterns for modern life.

The book's aim is practical and pastoral, urging young men to choose character, courage, and faith in a time of war and change. Its tone is earnest and fatherly, suited to students and graduates alike. For readers of devotional and campus literature, it is a thoughtful, old-fashioned call to live well while young.
33825-an-atheist-manifesto:
Joseph Lewis, a freethought writer, issued this manifesto in New York, copyrighted in 1954 with later editions in 1956 and 1958. He opens with a plain claim: whether a person believes in God makes all the difference, between truth and delusion, fact and guess. From there he argues that belief should rest on evidence, not on fear or custom.

Lewis, author of works on Voltaire, Paine, and the Bible in schools, writes in short, sharp sentences meant for a public reader. The manifesto defends atheism as a reasoned stance and attacks religious power in public life. It remains a clear statement of mid-century American freethought.
33946-a-stiptick-for-a-bleeding-nation-o:
A London pamphlet of 1721 offers a sharp cure for a bleeding nation: restore public credit and pay the national debts. Its author blames pride, luxury, corruption, and bribery for the country's woes, and warns that without reform the nation will rush toward ruin. The pamphlet urges readers to shake off the sores that corrupt the nation's vitals.

Piety, honesty, sincerity, and sobriety are held up as the way to a happy and flourishing people. Written in the wake of a financial crash, the tract speaks in urgent, moral terms. It gives modern readers a vivid sample of early eighteenth-century political preaching.
34019-the-popes-and-science-the-history-:
James J. Walsh wrote this history of the popes and science, tracing papal relations to science from the Middle Ages down to the nineteenth century. The volume runs to 540 pages and was priced at two dollars. Reviewers in Berlin and Cambridge praised it as a serious and scholarly argument.

Walsh takes up the long quarrel between church authority and new knowledge, case by case. He writes as a Catholic physician and scholar, aiming for fairness to both sides. The book remains a notable early American study of faith and science.
5136-around-the-world-on-a-bicycle-volum:
Thomas Stevens's first volume of Around the World on a Bicycle follows his ride from San Francisco to Teheran. Chapters cross the Sierra Nevada, the deserts of Nevada, Mormon country and the Rockies, the Great Plains to the Atlantic. The ride goes on through Germany, Austria, Hungary, Slavonia, Serbia, Bulgaria, and into Turkey.

Stevens rode a high bicycle in 1884, when few roads suited such a machine and strangers often stared. His account mixes road hardship, hospitality, and sharp observation of the lands he crossed. It remains a classic of bicycle travel, as well as an early story of going around the world by muscle power alone.
6466-the-intellectual-development-of-the:
John George Bourinot traces the intellectual development of the Canadian people in a historical review prepared as one of a series on the Dominion's social, political, and industrial progress. Canadian history divides into three periods, he argues: under the French regime, from the Conquest to the Union of 1840, and from 1840 to 1867, with a new period since Confederation. Intellectual lethargy marked New France, while United Empire Loyalists shaped the provinces' political and social life.

Parliamentary institutions, improved internal intercourse, growth of education, and political progress widened thought, and the professional and educated classes grew rapidly. A mid passage notes universities rising even in small provinces: Manitoba's university, Prince of Wales College after the 1860 Charlottetown visit, and Laval in Quebec, first suggested by Bishop Bourget of Montreal. Bourinot writes Canada's mind coming of age.
6652-the-humorous-poetry-of-the-english-:
James Parton gathers the best short humorous poems in English, from Chaucer to Saxe, with notes on each poet. Narratives, satires, enigmas, burlesques, parodies, epigrams, and epitaphs all appear, drawn from the Anti-Jacobin, Rejected Addresses, Ingoldsby Legends, Blackwood's, Bentley's, and Punch. More than two hundred epigrams alone fill the pages.

Wolcott, Cowper, Lamb, Thackeray, Swift, Scott, Holmes, Burns, Byron, Hood, and many more lend their wit. Parton leaves out poems too local or too tied to their day to travel well. The Humorous Poetry of the English Language is a thick, merry anthology, made for dipping into again and again.
7449-memoirs-of-general-lafayette-with-a:
Marie-Joseph-Paul-Yves-Roch-Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette, was the French hero of two revolutions. This volume joins his memoirs to the story of his last great visit to America. He arrived on August 15, 1824, and traveled through a nation eager to receive him. The tour ended at the celebration at Yorktown on October 19, 1824, the anniversary of the victory he had helped win.

The account records his reception by the people of the United States town by town, a farewell tour that became a national festival. Old soldiers, crowds, and officials all turned out for the general of their youth. The book preserves both Lafayette's own memories and the voice of a young republic honoring the man who had crossed an ocean to fight for its freedom.
7525-the-history-of-roman-literature-fro:
Charles Thomas Cruttwell, who inscribed this work to his former teacher, the Archdeacon of Middlesex, wrote his history of Roman literature for students and for general readers together. It runs from the earliest period to the death of Marcus Aurelius, covering the whole arc from rough early Latin to the polished literature of the empire. University and public school students were its first audience.

Cruttwell also hoped to reach those preparing for the Indian Civil Service and other advanced examinations, and any reader interested in the grand literature of Rome without being a professed scholar. The book moves author by author, genre by genre, through republic and empire. It remains a clear, old-fashioned survey, useful for anyone who wants the shape of Latin literature whole.
7787-a-complete-grammar-of-esperanto:
Ivy Kellerman's A Complete Grammar of Esperanto, with full vocabularies, teaches Zamenhof's planned language in plain, systematic form. A transcriber's note explains its 28 letters. English letters minus q, w, x, and y remain, plus six marked letters, with hats on c, g, h, j, and s, and a breve on u.

Where marks fail, Zamenhof's h-method or the clearer x-method can stand in, though the first blurs some sounds. The grammar that follows sets out sounds, word building, and use. It gives English speakers a full road into a language meant to cross borders without favoring any one nation.
7864-the-mahabharata-of-krishna-dwaipaya:
Kisari Mohan Ganguli's translation of the Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, made from Sanskrit prose between 1883 and 1896, aims to hold a mirror to its author. The translator's preface vows to keep the author's imagery and language, even at the cost of smooth English idiom and taste.

It is easy, Ganguli warns, to dish up Hindu ideas to suit English palates; harder to let them stand in their own form. This volume, scanned at sacred-texts.com, offers the great epic of the Bharata war, duty, and fate in full, faithful prose for readers new to India's central story.
7883-expositions-of-holy-scripture-secon:
Alexander MacLaren's Expositions of Holy Scripture, in this volume, moves from Second Kings chapter eight through Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, Job, Proverbs, and Ecclesiastes. Early sermons treat Hazael, impure zeal, Jehoiada and Joash, methodical giving, and the spirit of power.

Later expositions give a kingdom's epitaph, divided worship, Hezekiah as a pattern of devout life, the rediscovered law, and the end of Judah. David's choristers, drill and enthusiasm, and a charge to Solomon follow, with lessons on work and worship. Through close Bible reading, MacLaren draws plain moral lessons for daily faith and duty.
7965-the-mahabharata-of-krishna-dwaipaya:
Book 2 of the Mahabharata, the Sabha Parva, appears here in Kisari Mohan Ganguli's English prose translation from the Sanskrit. The book takes its name from the sabha, the great assembly hall built for King Yudhishthira. And it follows his royal consecration, the gathering of kings, and the events that lead toward the fateful dice match. The translation was published between 1883 and 1896.

Ganguli's version made the Sanskrit epic available to English readers in full, and this volume shows why the work endures. Councils and ceremonies give way to pride, rivalry, and choices with terrible costs. The Sabha Parva is where the Pandavas' fortunes turn, setting up the exile and war that follow. It is essential reading for anyone approaching the epic in order.
9071-the-non-christian-cross-an-enquiry-:
John Denham Parsons published this inquiry in London in 1896. It asks where the cross, later the sign of the Christian faith, came from before Christ. Parsons began as a youth with four puzzles, such as why John the Baptist, beheaded before Jesus died, is shown holding a cross in art.

He traces the sign through old rites, baptism, and pagan use, arguing that Christians took up an older mark. The book is earnest and learned, if now dated in parts. It still interests readers who ask how symbols travel across faiths and ages.
9077-hamlet-the-first-bad-quarto:
This file gives an early printed text of Shakespeare's Hamlet, known as the first bad quarto. It was printed in 1603, before the fuller texts that followed. Scholars call it bad because it is short, rough, and differs in lines and scenes from the Hamlet we know. It may stem from actors' memories of the play.

The Gutenberg note warns that this is an early file, made when proof methods were weak. A better edition exists as ebook 100. Even so, this text fascinates students of Shakespeare, showing how a great play first reached print in a flawed, pirated form.
939-the-life-of-thomas-telford-civil-eng:
Samuel Smiles, the biographer of engineers, tells the life of Thomas Telford, the Scottish builder of roads, bridges, canals, and harbours. Telford rose from a shepherd's son to president of the Institution of Civil Engineers. Smiles wrote lives of engineers to inspire young men to industry and thrift.

Smiles follows Telford's works across Britain, from the Caledonian Canal to the Menai Bridge, praising industry and perseverance. The life remains a classic of Victorian biography, and a tribute to the men who built modern Britain. Telford's Menai suspension bridge, opened in 1826, was a wonder of its age.
a-complete-grammar-of-esperanto: Ivy Kellerman Reed gives a complete grammar of Esperanto for English speaking learners. The book presents the language not as a thing apart but as a stepping stone to national tongues. It explains Esperanto's special letters, including those with circumflexes and the breve, and Zamenhof's fallback spellings. Reed's grammar serves both beginners and teachers of the planned language.
a-little-princess-being-the-whole-story-:
Frances Hodgson Burnett wrote this children's novel about Sara Crewe, a pupil at Miss Minchin's London boarding school. A summary printed with the text tells the arc plainly: Sara is left in poverty when her father dies in India, then rescued by a mysterious benefactor. The contents list nineteen chapters, from her arrival as the school's pampered show pupil through the diamond mines excitement to her years in the attic.

As a servant girl, Sara keeps her manners, her stories, and her kindness to the scullery maid Becky and the rat she befriends. Next door lives a sickly Indian gentleman whose servant watches the attic child with growing interest. Burnett builds the ending on that wall between the houses. The book endures as a story about holding one's dignity when fortune turns.
anguttara-nikaya-sujato:
Bhikkhu Sujato translated the Anguttara Nikaya, the Numbered Discourses, in a complete modern version. The collection is the fourth great book of the Sutta Pitaka. It holds 1,313 discourses arranged in eleven books by number.

Ones come first: one vital quality that changes everything for practice. Twos, threes, and onward climb the ladder to elevens by the end. Three poisons, four noble truths, and five hindrances fit the scheme naturally. The arrangement served monks who memorized the teaching orally for centuries. Sujato's translation makes the vast memory-library easy to walk through. English readers can now browse the whole numbered system freely online.
around-the-world-on-a-bicycle-volume-i-f:
Thomas Stevens's Around the World on a Bicycle, volume one, rides from San Francisco to Teheran. The original edition, copyrighted in 1887, ran to 547 pages with over a hundred illustrations. Stevens crossed the Sierras in his first chapter on a high-wheel bicycle, the penny-farthing ordinary. He was the first man to circle the globe on a wheel.

America falls behind through Nevada deserts, Wyoming snow, and prairie towns that turned out to stare. Europe follows: England, France, Germany, and the Balkans in succession. Turkey and Persia end the volume at Teheran, where winter stopped the wheel. Stevens writes as a San Francisco journalist, wry about discomfort and curious about everything. Yogurt, caravanserais, and brigands enter his phonetic spellings. The book remains the classic of bicycle travel, half feat and half reportage.
britannica-1911-acciajuoli-donato:
Donato Acciajuoli (1428-1478) was an Italian scholar born at Florence, famous for his learning, especially in Greek and mathematics, and for service to his native city. Florence trusted him with several important embassies before making him Gonfalonier, its chief magistrate, in 1473. He died at Milan while travelling to Paris to ask Louis XI of France for aid against Pope Sixtus IV.

Honesty marked his public life. His body was buried at public expense, and Florence provided portions for his daughters because his probity had left the family little fortune. His writings include a Latin translation of some of Plutarch's Lives, commentaries on Aristotle's Ethics and Politics, and lives of Hannibal, Scipio, and Charlemagne.
britannica-1911-accolti-benedetto:
Benedetto Accolti (1415-1466) was an Italian jurist and historian born at Arezzo in Tuscany, of a noble family distinguished for attainments in law. He taught jurisprudence at the university of Florence, and when the celebrated Poggio died he became chancellor of the Florentine republic in 1459. He died at Florence, leaving works in both his fields.

History brought his widest influence. With his brother Leonardo he wrote a Latin history of the first crusade in three books, printed at Venice in 1432 and later translated into Italian and French. Though the entry calls it of little interest in itself, it is said to have given Tasso the historic basis for his epic Jerusalem Delivered. His brother Francesco was also a noted jurist.
britannica-1911-aibonito:
Cool air, not size, gave Aibonito its special role in Porto Rico. The inland town stands near 2,200 feet up. Its climate, free of malaria, led officials to pick it as a health station where foreign newcomers could adjust and the sick could recover. Aibonito heads a municipal district of the same name in the electoral district of Guayama.

The road from San Juan to Ponce runs through it, twenty-five miles east-north-east of Ponce. In 1899 the town counted 2,085 people and the district 8,596. Coffee farms ring the town, and fine tobacco grows close by. The great storm of August 1899 hit Aibonito hard and did much damage.
britannica-1911-albertinelli-mariotto:
Albertinelli, Mariotto, an Italian painter of 1474 to 1515, receives a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Florence. His training tied his career to one partner above all, since he was a fellow-pupil of Fra Bartolommeo. The two became partners in their work, and many paintings came from their shared hand and shared workshop.

His chief paintings are in Florence, the city where he was born and trained. Among them one work stands out by name. The entry calls his Visitation of the Virgin, painted in 1503 and held at the Uffizi, his masterpiece. That picture shows the Virgin Mary visiting Elizabeth, a favourite subject of the period. Short as the notice is, it fixes the three facts by which Albertinelli is remembered: Florence, Fra Bartolommeo, and the Visitation of 1503.
britannica-1911-ayuntamiento:
Ayuntamiento is the Spanish name for the district a town council governs, for the council itself, and for the town-hall. The word comes from Latin adjungere, and first meant a meeting. In parts of Spain and Spanish America the council was also called cabildo, from capitulum, a chapter.

Its members mixed officials with regidores, regulators drawn in varying shares from hidalgos, the nobles, and pecheros, commoners who paid the personal tax called pecho. A royal judge, the corregidor, checked the body and in fact chaired it for good. The noble and commoner split has vanished in modern Spain, the entry notes, while the councils' powers and make-up have changed many times.
britannica-1911-azuni-domenico-alberto:
Azuni, Domenico Alberto (1749-1827), was an Italian jurist born at Sassari in Sardinia, who studied law at Sassari and Turin and became judge of the consulate at Nice in 1782. His dictionary of mercantile law appeared in 1786-1788, the start of a career spent on the law of trade and the sea.

His systematic work on Europe's maritime law came in 1795 and was later recast in French. In 1806 France put him on the commission drafting a general commercial code, and he presided over Genoa's appeal court. After Napoleon's fall, Victor Emmanuel called him home to Sardinia as consulate judge and university library director at Cagliari, where he died. His other writings include a history of maritime law and an account of Sardinia itself.
britannica-1911-badalocchio-sisto:
Badalocchio, Sisto, surnamed Rosa (1581-1647), was an Italian painter and engraver born at Parma. He belonged to the school of Annibale Carracci, who esteemed him highly for design, his drawing. With Lanfranco, another Carracci pupil, he shared the craft that made his best-known work.

That work is the engraving series called Raphael's Bible, the pair's principal claim on memory. Badalocchio's paintings are few, and the best of them are at Parma, his birthplace. He died at Bologna in 1647. Painter, engraver, Carracci's valued pupil, and partner in a famous print series: those are the points this short entry fixes for a minor master of the Italian Baroque age.
britannica-1911-barquisimeto:
Barquisimeto is a city of western Venezuela, capital of the state of Lara, on the Barquisimeto river, 101 miles by rail south-west of its Caribbean port of Tucacas. Its population was estimated at 40,000 in 1899. It stands in a small fertile valley of the Merida Cordilleras, 1,985 feet above the sea, with a temperate, healthy climate.

Coffee, sugar, cacao, and rum come down from the rich country around it for export, and the city serves as a distributing centre for its neighbours. Founded in 1522 by Juan de Villegas and first called Nueva Segovia, it grew on trade to 15,000 people by 1807. An earthquake destroyed it wholly on 26 March 1812, killing 1,500. The 1911 Britannica entry notes its recovery as one of the few Venezuelan cities to regain its standing.
britannica-1911-baumgarten-crusius-ludwi:
Ludwig Friedrich Otto Baumgarten-Crusius (1788–1842), a German Protestant divine born at Merseburg, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He entered Leipzig university in 1805 to study theology and philology, the study of language and texts. After teaching there as a junior lecturer, he became a professor of theology at Jena in 1812. He stayed at Jena for life, rising to head its theological faculty.

Breadth gave his teaching its worth. Apart from church history, he lectured on nearly all of theoretical theology: New Testament exegesis, biblical theology, dogmatic ethics, and the history of dogma. His deep learning and wide sympathies are praised in the entry. His books include a textbook of Christian morals, grounds of biblical theology, and textbooks on the history of dogma. The last and best of these was left unfinished and was completed from his notes by Karl Hase in 1846.
britannica-1911-benevento:
Benevento is a town and archbishop’s see of Campania, Italy, capital of its province, sixty miles by rail north-east of Naples. It stands on a hill four hundred feet up, where the Calore and Sabbato rivers meet. In 1901 the town held 17,227 people and the commune 24,137.

The site is ancient Beneventum, first called Maleventum and said to be founded by Diomedes. Chief town of the Samnites, it served Rome as a base against Pyrrhus, took a Latin colony in 268 B.C., and kept its worth through the Punic and Social wars. Six main roads met there, and its medieval walls, near two miles long, follow the ancient line Totila razed in 542.
britannica-1911-bitonto:
Bitonto, in ancient times Butunti, is a town and episcopal see in Apulia, Italy. It lies in the province of Bari, ten miles west of Bari by steam tramway. Its population in 1901 was 30,617. The town was of no importance in classical times, the 1911 Britannica entry says plainly. Its medieval walls are still preserved. The cathedral is singled out as one of the finest works of Apulian Romanesque building. It has escaped damage from later restorations, the entry adds.

The palazzo Sylos-Labini holds a fine Renaissance court dated 1502. Those two buildings carry the whole account of the town. The entry runs to a short paragraph of a few lines. No trade, history, or events are recorded in its space. Walls, cathedral, and the one palace court are the picture it leaves. Bitonto stands here as a quiet cathedral town west of Bari.
britannica-1911-bonfigli-benedetto:
Benedetto Bonfigli was an Italian painter of the 1400s from Perugia. The entry opens with the state of Umbrian art in his day. Until near the middle of that century the Umbrian school lagged far behind Florence and the north. Then, with Perugino and his followers, it rose all at once into the first rank.

Among those followers, the entry says, none holds a higher place than Bonfigli. His chief surviving works are a series of frescoes telling the life of St Louis of Toulouse. They are painted in the communal palace of Perugia, his home city. The short account gives his standing in the school and this one great work, and little more.
britannica-1911-brin-benedetto:
Benedetto Brin (1833–1898) was an Italian naval administrator born at Turin on 17 May 1833 who worked as a naval engineer with distinction until he was forty. In 1873 Admiral Saint-Bon, minister of marine, made him under-secretary. The pair fitted well: Saint-Bon conceived a type of ship, Brin drew the plans and directed the building.

Made minister of marine in 1876, he carried Saint-Bon's programme further into the first full scheme for growing the Italian fleet. The huge warships Italia and Dandolo were his work, though he later dropped their type for smaller, faster ships of the Varese and Garibaldi class. Across eleven years as minister he raised a near-absent naval industry into large private shipyards, engine works and steel and gun plants. In 1892 he joined the Giolitti cabinet as foreign minister.
britannica-1911-casale-monferrato:
Casale Monferrato is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town and episcopal see of Piedmont, Italy, in the province of Alessandria. It lies in the plain on the right bank of the Po, 377 feet above sea level, 21 miles north north west of Alessandria by rail. The town counted 18,874 people in 1901, and its commune 31,370. Rail lines and steam tramways tie it to Mortara, Vercelli, Chivasso, and Asti.

The Lombard Romanesque cathedral, first founded in 742 and rebuilt in the early twelfth century, holds good pictures, and the church of S. Domenico is a fine Renaissance building. About ten miles away stands the Sacro Monte di Crea, with eighteen chapels of terra cotta statue groups on its slopes. Charlemagne gave the town to the church of Vercelli, and it won its liberty from Frederick Barbarossa. It was sacked in 1215, rebuilt and fortified in 1220, and passed under its marquises in 1292.
britannica-1911-cellini-benvenuto:
Benvenuto Cellini (1500–1571) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an Italian artist, metal worker, and sculptor born in Florence. His father, Giovanni, made musical instruments and meant his son for the same trade. Benvenuto's bent for metal work proved stronger. At fifteen he was apprenticed to the goldsmith Antonio di Sandro, called Marcone. A street fray brought him six months of banishment to Siena.

After work in Siena and Bologna, Cellini reached Rome at nineteen. A silver casket, candlesticks, and a vase for the bishop of Salamanca brought him to the notice of Pope Clement VII. His gold medallion of Leda and the Swan won further fame. He also played the flute and joined the pope's court musicians. The entry turns next to his conduct in the attack on Rome by the constable de Bourbon in 1527. It praises his bravery and skill in that crisis.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrea-del-sa:
Andrea del Sarto, born Andrea d'Agnolo at Florence in 1486, dead there in 1531, took his surname from his tailor father. He studied first under the obscure G. Barile, then from 1498 in Piero di Cosimo's studio. He visited Rome briefly. Vasari says that, had he stayed to study its masterpieces, he would have surpassed every artist of his day. Diffident, he felt a stranger there and hurried back to Florence.

Despite his short career he produced many frescoes and easel pictures. From 1509 he decorated the Annunziata cloister for the Servites, with five scenes from Saint Philip Benizi's life and, in 1525, the Madonna of the Sack. In 1514 he began ten frescoes in the cloister of the Scalzo. Later works include the Madonna of the Harpies at the Uffizi, a Virgin with Saints at Berlin, and a Pieta at Vienna. Francis I bought two of them and drew him to Paris.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-atto:
Atto, probably born at Milan, was a faithful backer of Pope Gregory VII in his fight against simoniac clergy, priests who bought church office. He was made Cardinal of San Marco. He stood by at the retractation of Berengarius at the Roman synod of 1079, and signed the decrees of the synod of 1081. He may also have served as Bishop of Praeneste, though the entry leaves that point open.

Cardinal Mai later published, under Atto's name and from a Vatican manuscript, a Breviarium Canonum. It is a mixed store of moral and church-law decrees, genuine and forged, running from Pope Clement I to Gregory the Great. It deals in particular with clerical rights and duties, church acts, the sacraments, censures, and jurisdiction. The entry closes by noting other cardinals of the same name, discussed in an anonymous eighteenth-century tract on the Attos.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-barquisimeto:
Barquisimeto is a diocese in Venezuela, its city the capital of Lara State, about 161 miles southwest of Caracas. Founded by Spaniards in 1552 as Nueva Segovia, it ranks among South America's oldest Spanish possessions. An 1812 earthquake almost entirely destroyed it, and its population runs about 30,000, though some authorities give less.

The diocese was erected in 1847 over Lara, Carabobo, and Falcon. By a 1907 decree, the bishop's residence moved to Valencia, and the boundaries were rearranged. It now meets the Caribbean on the north and west, Mérida to the south, and Calabozo, Zamora, and Guiana to the east. It counts 528,215 Catholics, 68 priests, and 110 churches and chapels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benevento:
Benevento, an ancient city of Campania in southern Italy, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Founded by the Samnites as Maleventum, it passed to Rome after the defeat of Pyrrhus in 275 BC and took its present name. A Roman colony followed, enlarged by Augustus, whose age is recalled by the marble arch of Trajan still standing.

Medieval and modern turns fill the rest: capture by Totila, Norman fealty to Pope Leo IX, centuries as papal territory, and annexation to the Kingdom of Italy in 1860. The future Pope Leo XIII served there as papal delegate. The entry closes with its archdiocese, its suffragan sees, and its native popes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-john-de-br:
Blessed John de Britto, a Jesuit martyr in India, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in Lisbon in 1647 and raised at court, he was martyred in India in 1693. Joining the Jesuits at fifteen, he chose Madura in southern India as his field, reaching Goa in September 1673.

After thirty days of Ignatian retreat near Cranganore, he entered the Kshatriya caste's world in dress and diet, wearing yellow cotton and eating no meat or wine. On foot across the Ghats he reached the Cauvery delta and mastered the local language. Arrest for preaching ended in martyrdom. The entry presents a courtier turned Indian missionary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-casale-monfer:
Casale Monferrato is a diocese suffragan to Vercelli, set in Alessandria province in Piedmont on the River Po. The ancient Bodincomagus, it has been a stronghold since Lombard times. King Liutprand enlarged it, and Otto II made it a marquisate town for the sons of Aleran, Duke of Saxony. It later passed to the Palaeologi, then in 1533 to the Gonzaga, to France from 1681 to 1706, and to Savoy in 1713.

Sixtus IV created the see in 1474, after it belonged to Asti, with Bernardino de Tebaldeschi as first bishop. His successor Gian Giorgio Paleologo also governed the marquisate for a minor nephew. Notable bishops include Benedetto Erba, zealous for children's instruction and Tridentine reform beside Charles Borromeo. Giulio Careta founded a priests' oratory and nursed plague victims in 1630. The diocese counts 200,500 people in 140 parishes, with a cathedral ranked among the finest Lombard monuments.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-civitavecchia:
Civitavecchia, an important fortified Mediterranean seaport in Rome province, keeps fortifications and piers dating from Emperor Trajan. Popes from Eugene the Fourth to Urban the Eighth improved it under their temporal rule. Pope Cornelius was exiled to Centumcellae, the city's ancient name, during the Gallus persecution, and catacombs have been found there. Epictetus, its bishop, attended the Council of Arles in 314, while a later Epictetus, a rabid Arian, counselled Emperor Constantius badly.

The see was suppressed in 1086 and joined first to Toscanella, then in 1193 to Viterbo. Leo the Twelfth restored it in 1825 with Porto and Santa Rufina, and in 1854 it was united instead with Corneto. Corneto, near the ruins of Tarquinii, once capital of southern Etruria, shows its advanced civilisation in painted pottery from its many tombs. Its Christianity came not from Rome or by sea but from neighbouring Bolsena. The diocese counts 29,700 Catholics in twelve parishes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dominic-soto:
Dominic Soto was a Dominican theologian born at Segovia in 1494 who died at Salamanca in 1560. He studied first at home, then at Alcala under Saint Thomas of Villanova, and later at Paris, where he took a degree in philosophy. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how he returned to Alcala about 1520 as professor of philosophy at San Ildefonso. There he won a full triumph for moderate realism over the errors of nominalism.

Already famed as a teacher, he gave up his chair in 1524 for the religious life, retreating first to Montserrat. His commentaries on the Sentences and on Romans, printed at Salamanca and Antwerp, kept his name alive in the schools. The entry cites Echard and Hurter among the sources for a career cut between the lecture hall and the cloister.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fernao-mendes:
Fernao Mendes Pinto was a Portuguese traveller and classic prose writer of the East. Born about 1509, he sailed to the East Indies in 1537. For twenty-one years he wandered the Far East by sea. Shipwrecked and enslaved at times, he survived to tell his tale.

Pinto first told Europe of Japan's riches and built the first settlement near Yokohama in 1548. His Peregrinacao, printed in 1614, became a Portuguese classic. Some call it romance, but its substantial honesty is now generally admitted. He wrote from memory, setting down vivid impressions rather than bare facts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-filipo-archin:
Filipo Archinto was an Italian theologian, diplomatist, and churchman. Born at Milan in 1500, he took his law doctorate at Padua at twenty. Paul III made him governor of the City of Rome and vice-chamberlain apostolic. He became bishop of the Holy Sepulchre and later of Saluzzo.

Archinto presided at Trent for the pope before the council's transfer to Bologna. St Ignatius gained a powerful protector in him in the Society's early years. Paul IV named him for Milan's archbishopric, but death prevented his installation. His theological works include De fide et sacramentis of 1545.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-batt:
Giovanni Battista Salvi da Sassoferrato was a painter born at Sassoferrato in 1609, who died at Rome in 1689, where he spent most of his life. His father Tarquinio taught him first, and at Naples he studied under Domenichino and through him the Carracci. A Catholic Encyclopedia article presents a painter of Madonnas whose tender sweetness rivaled Carlo Dolci.

Where many seventeenth-century Virgins look cold and distant from the Child, his Madonnas show a mother's heart, with a pleasing intimacy and naiveté. His masterpiece, Our Lady of the Rosary with St. Dominic and St. Catherine, was painted for the Princess de Rossano. Finished in 1643, it hangs in St. Sabina in Rome. His Madonnas fill museums from London and Paris to St. Petersburg and Vienna.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-cler:
Giovanni Clericato was a canonist born at Padua in 1633, who died in 1717. Of English descent, his family name, written in several forms, probably came from Clark. The charity of a pious woman let him follow his strong bent for study. Raised to the priesthood, he came to rank among the ablest men of his time in ecclesiastical jurisprudence. A Catholic Encyclopedia article holds his name in honor in Italian church literature.

Cardinal Barbarigo, whose life Clericato later wrote, named him vicar-general for Padua. His many works on civil and canon law include Decisiones Sacramentales, published in 1727 and again in three volumes in 1757, which won the praise of Benedict XIV. Those books kept his name alive among canon lawyers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-grosseto:
Grosseto, a suffragan diocese of Siena, takes its name from the Tuscan town at the mouth of the Ombrone river in the unhealthy Maremma country. Its story starts in 803, when the Aldobrandeschi counts held it as a fief, it grew as older Rusellae and Vetulonia decayed and passed to Sienese control in 1224. It kept its fortress walls and bastions as marks of its time as a stronghold.

Its church story runs from Rusellae, an episcopal city from the fifth century, to the transfer of the see to Grosseto by Innocent II in 1138. The Romanesque cathedral, finished in 1295 with a striped marble front, anchors a roll of bishops that includes a Trent figure, Marcantonio Campeggio. The entry closes with 26 parishes and 30,250 faithful.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gugliemo-sirl:
Calabrian scholar Guglielmo Sirleto, born at Guardavalle in 1514, became one of the Council of Trent's most trusted behind-the-scenes minds. A friend of Marcello Cervino, later Marcellus II, he wrote full reports on the council's questions, catalogued the Vatican Library's Greek manuscripts, and brought out a fresh Vulgate edition.

Made cardinal in 1565 and Vatican librarian in 1570, he steered the scientific work Trent had ordered: the Roman Catechism, the reform of Breviary and Missal, and a new Roman Martyrology. A lover of Greek culture who encouraged reunion with the East, he taught Greek and Hebrew at Rome, counting St. Charles Borromeo among his pupils, and died attended by St. Philip Neri.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-haito:
Basle's Bishop Haito, born of a Swabian noble family in 763, entered Reichenau at five, headed its school under Abbot Waldo, and became abbot and bishop together about 806. Trusted by Charlemagne, he carried a diplomatic mission to Constantinople in 811 and rebuilt the cathedrals of Basle and Reichenau. He issued guidance for clergy and people before resigning both offices in 823 through infirmity.

His writings include a lost account of the Constantinople journey and the Visio Wettini of 824, in which the dying schoolmaster Wettin tours hell, purgatory, and heaven under an angel's guidance. That vision was later versified by Walafrid Strabo, and the Capitulare Haitonis, twenty-five chapters of diocesan discipline, was probably issued at a synod.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hatto:
Mainz Archbishop Hatto, born of a Swabian noble family about 850, was monk, abbot, and kingmaker in a Germany pulling toward fragmentation. Educated at Ellwangen, a Benedictine at Fulda, abbot of Reichenau in 888 and Ellwangen a year later, he won King Arnulf's trust and the archbishopric of Mainz in September 891.

His guiding aim was a united German kingdom under a strong king. This made dukes who wanted independent states hate him. After Arnulf's death he steered the election of the six-year-old Louis the Child and governed during his short reign. He then secured Conrad I of Franconia as king and served as his chief counsellor until his death in 913. He has been maligned ever since by tales of treachery and the mouse-tower fable, both without foundation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hernando-de-s:
Hernando de Soto was a Spanish explorer and conqueror, born in Extremadura around 1496 or 1500 and dead on the banks of the Mississippi in June 1542. He served in Central America, joined Pizarro's conquest of Peru as second in command, and became the first Spaniard to speak with the Inca Atahualpa. He grew disgusted when Pizarro had Atahualpa killed despite a large ransom.

De Soto then won the governorship of Cuba and leave to conquer Florida. He sailed in 1538, rebuilt Havana, and marched north through the American southeast with hundreds of horses, seeking riches and a route to New Spain. He died of fever before reaching it, and his men hid his body in the great river. The entry traces a career of bold marches, harsh clashes, and a quest that outran its leader.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ignacio-de-ar:
Ignacio de Arbieto was a Jesuit, born at Madrid in February 1585 and dead at Lima in 1670. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1603, and Lima saw his priestly ordination in 1612. Quito in Ecuador gave him its philosophy chair first; Arequipa came next, and Lima last, where he died.

Over twenty-five interrupted years he taught in Peru, then gave his final years to a History of Peru and its Jesuit foundations. That manuscript lies at Lima's National Archives in a hopeless state of decay. The entry preserves what is known of a scholar-teacher whose chief work survives only as a crumbling manuscript.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-il-tintoretto:
Jacopo Robusti, called Il Tintoretto or the little dyer, was a Venetian painter born in 1518 and dead there in 1594. His father dyed cloth, which explains the nickname. Young Jacopo played the harp well, yet painting drew him even more. His parents placed him with old Titian as an apprentice, but the ambitious youth soon opened his own studio.

He aimed to remake Venetian painting altogether. He kept its brilliant, harmonious colour and graceful forms, and joined to them Florentine and Roman strengths: anatomy strong in the nude, dramatic staging, moving poses, and bold light-and-shade contrasts. Ridolfi, his biographer, sums up the program as Michelangelo's drawing wedded to Titian's colouring.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-in-petto:
Reserved “in the breast” is the plain sense of this Italian phrase, used when a pope names cardinals in secret. At a consistory, the formal meeting where cardinals are created, a pope may add that he is holding back one or more names to reveal later. This entry explains what that secret naming did and did not do.

Until their names were made public, cardinals kept in petto held no rights of office. If the pope died first they never joined the Sacred College. Once proclaimed at a later consistory, they ranked from the date of their first naming and drew pay from that date.
